The Phase III rotor was designed to have a steeper average suction surface angle in the supersonic region ahead of the shock than the baseline rotor.
The throat margin was set at essentially 5% in the outer 80% of the Phase III blade, except for locally at the tip where the margin is a little over 6%.
The incidence angles for the Phase III rotor were kept very close to the baseline rotor values.
A higher efficiency was assumed for the outer 80% of the Phase III rotor compared to the baseline.

The streamline work input distribution for the Phase III rotor was iteratively adjusted to obtain a static pressure distribution similar to the baseline rotor, but with a higher pressure level in the outer portion.
The stator incidence angles were lower in the outer 40% of the span for the Phase III rotor compared to the baseline.
The location of maximum airfoil thickness is 70% of length at the tip and 56% at the hub for the Phase III rotor, which is the same as the baseline rotor.
The streamsurface tip section of the Phase III rotor had greater suction surface and meanline curvatures in the region of the cascade mouth compared to the baseline rotor.

The Phase III and Phase IV rotors were designed to have smaller throat areas than the baseline in order to get more definitive data on the effect of the suction surface shape ahead of the leading edge passage shock.
The circumferential average flow solution and stream surface blade section analysis from the baseline rotor design were used as a starting point for the Phase III rotor design.
A method of characteristics program was used to analyze the flow in the cascade induction region for the Phase III rotor design.
The Phase III rotor was designed under Contract F33615-80-C-2059 for the United States Air Force Systems Command, Air Force Wright Aeronautical Laboratories.
The work on the Phase III rotor design was performed over a period of one year starting in September 1980.
The goal of the overall program was to aerodynamically define five rotor designs, all parametrically related to a baseline design, which could be evaluated by future testing.
The purpose was to define the sensitivity of transonic blade rows to several design variables.
